title: Keep Each Value At Most Twice
statement:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. Thin it out in place so that every value appears at most twice, keeping the survivors in their original sorted order.

Let k be how many elements survive. After your function runs, the first k slots of nums must hold exactly those survivors. Anything after slot k − 1 is ignored, and the array keeps its length. Use O(1) extra memory: do not build a second array.

The function returns nothing. The checker works out k itself and reads the first k slots of your array.

examples.why: Runs longer than two are cut to two; the single 5 stays. k = 5.
The second copy of 0 must stay. Comparing only with the previous slot would wrongly drop it or keep a third 3.
No value repeats, so nothing moves.

constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Write survivors to the front with a write pointer, like squeezing out repeats, but allow two copies.
When deciding whether nums[i] may stay, which already-written slot should you compare it with?
Compare with the slot two places behind the write pointer. If nums[i] equals it, two copies are already written; otherwise copy nums[i] to the write slot.

explain.intuition:
Keep a write pointer w: everything before it is the finished, thinned-out prefix. Because the array is sorted, equal values are next to each other, so a third copy would have to equal the value written two slots back, at nums[w − 2].

That single comparison is the whole rule. If nums[i] ≠ nums[w − 2], the prefix holds fewer than two copies of it, so write it. Comparing with the written prefix rather than the original neighbours matters, because the original slots get overwritten as you go.
steps: For each value x in nums, from left to right:
If w < 2 or x ≠ nums[w − 2], set nums[w] = x and increase w.
Otherwise skip x: two copies are already kept.
When the loop ends, the first w slots are the answer.
pitfalls: Comparing nums[i] with nums[i − 2] in the original positions. Those slots may already be overwritten, so a run can slip through with three copies.
Comparing only with the previous kept value. That allows one copy per value, not two.
Splicing elements out of the array. Each splice shifts the tail, which turns the pass into O(n²).

solutions.title: Splice out every third copy
solutions.idea: Walk the array and delete an element whenever it is the third copy in a row. Simple, but each delete shifts the rest of the array.

solutions.title: Write pointer, compare two back
solutions.idea: A value may be written unless it equals the value written two slots earlier.

followups: Generalise to at most k copies of each value. What changes in the loop?
The array is not sorted. Can you still keep at most two copies of each value in one pass, and what extra memory does that need?
lcTitle: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
